transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-22 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 min
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Lee (Redwood SE), Carlos (CTO - NexaHealth), Priya (ML Eng), Sam (Product), Aisha (Security)

Auto-generated Summary: Demo of Redwood Hosted API focused on chat/text generation basics. Showed streaming and param controls, and discussed retry/backoff and idempotency. Customer asked about security, data retention, private options.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um i'm maya from redwood inference, i'll kick off super quick, jordan will do the demo and lee will chime in on ops and security, and maybe we go 30 to 40 minutes and leave time for q's.
[00:20] Carlos: thanks maya, yep we are excited, i'm carlos, cto at nexahealth, quick context - we have a clinical notes summarization flow and want to add a chat assistant for clinicians. Primary concerns are latency <200ms for short prompts, cost, and patient data privacy.
[00:40] Maya: perfect. quick qual: are you currently using any hosted LLMs?
[00:45] Priya: we're prototyping with openai for TTR but costs are ramping, and we saw some variability in latency from region, also curious about streaming.
[01:05] Jordan: cool. i'll show the hosted api path which is the fastest to onboard. first slide, quick API overview, simple REST/SDK, endpoints for chat, text-generation, embeddings and reranking.
[01:30] Jordan: here's a basic chat request, system messages, user messages, we send to /v1/chat/completions, you get back delta chunks if streaming is enabled.
[01:45] Sam: real quick, streaming means we can start rendering tokens as they arrive?
[01:50] Jordan: exactly, you get partial tokens in a chunked stream — good for perceived latency. for clinician workflows streaming is often nice because UI can show progressive answer.
[02:10] Jordan: demo time, i'll do a live curl example. (typing) curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d '{"model":"rwd-chat-1","messages":[{"role":"system","content":"You are a clinical assistant"},{"role":"user","content":"Summarize the patient visit in three bullets"}] , "stream": true, "temperature": 0.2}'
[02:40] [streaming output noise / partial tokens] 
[03:00] Priya: oh neat, in the stream i see the partial sentences come through, are there guarantees about order or chunk size?
[03:10] Jordan: order is preserved; chunks are emitted as tokens are produced. chunk size depends on tokenization and model latency. occasionally the transcriber here says 'KV cash' instead of 'KV cache' ha, but under the hood the runtime is managing kv cache for faster generation.
[03:35] Carlos: for our use case we need to ensure token-level cost is predictable; how do you expose that?
[03:45] Maya: console has token-level breakdowns per request, per model, and cost estimates. we can also help pick a quantized model variant if latency cost tradeoff is needed.
[04:10] Jordan: param demo — temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences, and presence/penalty. for most deterministic clinical summaries we recommend low temperature (0-0.3), top_p 0.9 or disabled, and setting max_tokens to cap cost.
[04:40] Priya: any advice on system messages? we have PHI - should we prefer system-level templates?
[04:50] Jordan: yes system messages are good for behavior constraints. but for PHI you should also consider data handling options — hosted stores logs for X days by default, but you can disable retention and opt for dedicated/private deployment if retention policy must be zero. we'll send the security pack.
[05:15] Aisha: can you speak to encryption and KMS?
[05:20] Lee: sure — we support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) for dedicated/private, hosted has encryption at rest with our KMS; for stricter controls we offer private deployment with KMS integration and audit logs. we'll attach the SOC2/ISO docs.
[05:40] Jordan: back to APIs — retries. if you see 5xx or 429, pattern is exponential backoff with jitter. recommended client-side: idempotency keys for non-streaming or transient submit operations; for streaming we recommend a resume token pattern where feasible. sample code in the SDK shows automatic retries with backoff.
[06:10] Maya: it's worth noting that retries and at-least-once behavior can re-generate tokens, so cost accounting matters — we can advise on retry budget per minute.
[06:25] Carlos: can you demonstrate the SDK's streaming client?
[06:30] Jordan: yep, i'll switch to the node example in the console. (screen share) code snippet: const stream = client.chat.stream({ model: 'rwd-chat-1', messages, temperature: 0.2 }); stream.on('data', chunk => { render(chunk.delta) }) stream.on('end', ()=> console.log('done'))
[07:05] Priya: in case of intermittent network blips, does the SDK automatically resume?
[07:10] Jordan: not automatic resume in the stream itself; the SDK will surface errors and you should implement a resume or re-request logic at the app layer. for short interruptions many customers re-request the tail and dedupe. we can provide sample logic.
[07:35] Sam: about params, can you talk about batching? we have bursts from triage teams.
[07:40] Jordan: hosted supports request-level batching on some endpoints; more importantly the runtime does continuous batching to improve throughput. batching helps throughput but may add ms to first token; tradeoff is adjustable via route settings.
[08:05] Jordan: show Console now — per-route dashboards, token breakdowns, latency p95/p50, and cost analysis. you can filter by model version and timeframe.
[08:30] [shared link posted in chat: https://console.redwood.ai/demo/nexahealth (demo link - not production)]
[08:45] Carlos: great. can we pin a model version and do canary rollouts?
[08:50] Maya: yes, you can pin versions, do canaries and automatic fallback to a cheaper variant if latency or errors exceed thresholds.
[09:05] Priya: curious about quantized models for cost — do you support int8/int4 for hosted?
[09:10] Jordan: yes we have quantized variants in the model catalog; they come with performance profiles. we can recommend a quantization profile based on your prompt length distribution. that's part of Redwood Optimize.
[09:35] Priya: if we start hosted but later want private, how hard is migration?
[09:40] Lee: we provide the same API surface and config layer, so migration is mostly about networking and key management. customers often pilot on hosted and then move to dedicated or private when they need specific controls.
[10:05] Carlos: any limitations on PII/PHI in logs? default retention?
[10:10] Maya: default hosted retention is 30 days for logs; you can opt out or configure shorter retention. dedicated has configurable retention and private gives you full control. we'll include the exact retention matrix in the docs.
[10:30] Sam: ok let's talk reliability SLAs.
[10:35] Maya: hosted has best-effort, dedicated has SLA options with 99.9 uptime depending on plan. enterprise plans include support escalation.
[10:50] Jordan: small deep dive: streaming architecture - the model runtime emits token deltas via a websocket or chunked HTTP stream; we do kernel selection to optimize for short-sequence latency. sometimes the transcript auto caption mislabels 'kernel' as 'colonel' — transcription lol.
[11:20] [15 minute skip for live demo interactions - paraphrased]
[26:30] Jordan: showed a sample benchmark comparing rwd-chat-1 vs rwd-chat-lite; for short prompts rwd-chat-1 p50 ~110ms, rwd-chat-lite p50 ~85ms but quality tradeoffs at low temps.
[27:00] Priya: can we run this with our prompt set?
[27:05] Jordan: absolutely, jordan will send the script. the script uses concurrent requests of 10, measures p50/p95 and token usage per prompt.
[27:20] Carlos: on billing — is it per token or per request?
[27:25] Maya: per-token for generation + per-request fee for some features; console shows per-request cost breakdown. we'll include sample cost estimates for your prompt set.
[28:00] Aisha: security question: SSO and audit logs?
[28:05] Lee: we support SAML/SSO, RBAC, and detailed audit trails in both hosted and dedicated. private gives you more granular network isolation.
[28:35] Priya: any vendor lock-in concerns with function calling or structured outputs?
[28:40] Jordan: we support function/tool calling patterns; the payloads are JSON and straightforward to map. we also have schema enforcement in the SDK if you need strict typed outputs.
[29:10] Sam: what's the typical timeline to pilot?
[29:15] Maya: usually a 2-4 week pilot: week 0 setup, week1-2 run benchmarks and iterate, week3 evaluate quality and cost. for regulated corp we do an extra security review.
[29:40] Carlos: ok sounds good. next steps?
[29:45] Maya: recap — we'll send pricing + security docs, jordan will send benchmarking script and example streaming code, you send 10 prompts and target latency. then we'll sync for pilot kickoff.
[30:00] Priya: one final quick question about retries: if we get a 429, is there a recommended cap on retries?
[30:05] Jordan: yes we recommend exponential backoff and a total retry budget (e.g., 3 attempts with exponential backoff starting at 100ms plus jitter). for rate-limited bursts we can enable burst capacity on dedicated.
[30:30] Carlos: any example of idempotency key usage?
[30:35] Jordan: for non-streaming replaceable ops you can send an idempotency_key header; we store request-id to dedupe duplicate requests for N minutes. sample in the SDK.
[31:00] [Q&A finishes; short wrap]
[32:00] Maya: thanks all — we'll follow up with the attachments. any blockers?
[32:10] Carlos: none; team will pull together prompts and security contact will review the pack.
[32:20] Maya: great. thanks again.
